   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$

Fix positive integers $d,n,H,m$, training inputs $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\|x_i\|_2=1$, labels $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$, an analytic nonpolynomial activation $\sigma$ satisfying $|\sigma(0)|<\infty$ and finite Lipschitz constants for $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$, and the positive finite normalization $c_\sigma=(\mathbb E_{Z\sim N(0,1)}[\sigma(Z)^2])^{-1}$. A fully connected network of width $m$ and depth $H$ is the finite feedforward recurrence

$$x^{(0)}=x,\qquad x^{(h)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(1\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm fc}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

where $W^{(1)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}$, $W^{(h)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for $h\ge2$, $a\in\mathbb R^m$, and $\sigma$ acts coordinatewise. The residual network uses the same first layer and then

$$x^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(1)}x),\qquad x^{(h)}=x^{(h-1)}+\frac{c_{\rm res}}{H\sqrt m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(2\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm res}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

with $0<c_{\rm res}<1$. In either architecture, random initialization means all entries of all matrices $W^{(h)}$ and of $a$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables; all these entries are trained by full-batch gradient descent. The empirical quadratic loss is $L(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(f(x_i,\theta)-y_i)^2$.

For the fully connected architecture and the same fixed data, define the population matrices by

$$K_{ij}^{(0)}=\langle x_i,x_j\rangle.$$

For $1\le h<H$, let $(U_{ij}^{(h)},V_{ij}^{(h)})$ be a centered bivariate normal vector with covariance

$$A_{ij}^{(h)}=\begin{pmatrix}K_{ii}^{(h-1)}&K_{ij}^{(h-1)}\\K_{ji}^{(h-1)}&K_{jj}^{(h-1)}\end{pmatrix},$$

and put $K_{ij}^{(h)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(U_{ij}^{(h)})\sigma(V_{ij}^{(h)})]$. For $h=H$, use the same bivariate-normal definition with $A_{ij}^{(H)}$ formed from $K^{(H-1)}$, and set

$$K_{ij}^{(H)}=c_\sigma K_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(U_{ij}^{(H)})\sigma'(V_{ij}^{(H)})].$$

When $H=1$, this last formula uses $K^{(0)}$ directly and there are no intermediate activation-covariance matrices. For the fully connected theorem, this terminal matrix is denoted $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$.

For the residual architecture with $H\ge2$, use a separate sequence $S^{(h)}$ and mean vector $b^{(h)}$. Set $S^{(0)}=K^{(0)}$. For $G^{(0)}\sim N_n(0,S^{(0)})$, put

$$S_{ij}^{(1)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})\sigma(G_j^{(0)})],\qquad b_i^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma}\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})].$$

Write $\alpha=c_{\rm res}/H$. For $2\le h<H$, take a fresh centered Gaussian vector $G^{(h-1)}$ with covariance $S^{(h-1)}$, put $\mu_i^{(h-1)}=\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})]$, and define

$$S_{ij}^{(h)}=S_{ij}^{(h-1)}+\alpha\bigl(b_i^{(h-1)}\mu_j^{(h-1)}+b_j^{(h-1)}\mu_i^{(h-1)}\bigr)+\alpha^2\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})\sigma(G_j^{(h-1)})],\qquad b_i^{(h)}=b_i^{(h-1)}+\alpha\mu_i^{(h-1)}.$$

For $G\sim N_n(0,S^{(H-1)})$, define the residual terminal matrix by

$$K_{{\rm res},ij}^{(H)}=\frac{c_{\rm res}^2}{H^2}S_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(G_i)\sigma'(G_j)].$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

A fully connected network of width $m$ and depth $H$ is the finite feedforward recurrence

$$x^{(0)}=x,\qquad x^{(h)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(1\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm fc}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

where $W^{(1)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}$, $W^{(h)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for $h\ge2$, $a\in\mathbb R^m$, and $\sigma$ acts coordinatewise. The residual network uses the same first layer and then

$$x^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(1)}x),\qquad x^{(h)}=x^{(h-1)}+\frac{c_{\rm res}}{H\sqrt m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(2\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm res}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

with $0<c_{\rm res}<1$. In either architecture, random initialization means all entries of all matrices $W^{(h)}$ and of $a$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables; all these entries are trained by full-batch gradient descent. The empirical quadratic loss is $L(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(f(x_i,\theta)-y_i)^2$.

For the fully connected architecture and the same fixed data, define the population matrices by

$$K_{ij}^{(0)}=\langle x_i,x_j\rangle.$$

For $1\le h<H$, let $(U_{ij}^{(h)},V_{ij}^{(h)})$ be a centered bivariate normal vector with covariance

$$A_{ij}^{(h)}=\begin{pmatrix}K_{ii}^{(h-1)}&K_{ij}^{(h-1)}\\K_{ji}^{(h-1)}&K_{jj}^{(h-1)}\end{pmatrix},$$

$$K_{ij}^{(H)}=c_\sigma K_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(U_{ij}^{(H)})\sigma'(V_{ij}^{(H)})].$$

When $H=1$, this last formula uses $K^{(0)}$ directly and there are no intermediate activation-covariance matrices. For the fully connected theorem, this terminal matrix is denoted $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$.

For the residual architecture with $H\ge2$, use a separate sequence $S^{(h)}$ and mean vector $b^{(h)}$. Set $S^{(0)}=K^{(0)}$. For $G^{(0)}\sim N_n(0,S^{(0)})$, put

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

By [F2] and [F4], $\mu$ is finite; because $\sigma(Z)\ge\log 2$ when $Z\ge0$ and the standard normal density is positive on $(0,1)$, $\mu>0$. Expanding this finite square and using $\mathbb E s=\mu$ yields $\mathbb E[s^2]>\mu^2$. Therefore $0<\rho<1$.

Let $U=\operatorname{span}\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$. By [F5], $\mathbb R^d=U\oplus U^\perp$, and [F6] supplies an orthonormal basis of $U^\perp$. Joining it to $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ gives the columns of an orthogonal matrix $Q$. By [F7], $W^{(1)}Q$ has the same iid Gaussian law as $W^{(1)}$, so all coordinates $W^{(1)}_{r\cdot}x_i$ are independent standard normals. Thus $\mathbb E[(\Phi\Phi^T)_{ii}]=c_\sigma\mathbb E[s^2]=1$, while for $i\ne j$, $\mathbb E[(\Phi\Phi^T)_{ij}]=c_\sigma\mu^2=\rho$. Therefore $\mathbb E[\Phi\Phi^T]=(1-\rho)I_n+\rho\mathbf1\mathbf1^T$, and its quadratic form in the unit vector $e$ is $1+(n-1)\rho$.

Conditional on the hidden weights, $e^Tu=e^T\Phi a$ is a centered normal random variable with variance $S=e^T\Phi\Phi^Te\ge0$, by [F1] and [F3]. The nonnegative random variable $S$ has expectation $1+(n-1)\rho>\rho n/2$, so the event $S>\rho n/2$ has positive probability; otherwise its expectation would be at most $\rho n/2$. On this event, for any fixed $C>0$, the conditional probability of $|e^Tu|>C\sqrt n$ is at least $P\{|Z|>C\sqrt{2/\rho}\}>0$. Averaging over the hidden weights proves positive unconditional probability. Since $e$ is a unit vector, write $u=(e^Tu)e+(u-(e^Tu)e)$; the summands are orthogonal, so $\|u\|_2^2=|e^Tu|^2+\|u-(e^Tu)e\|_2^2\ge|e^Tu|^2$. Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;:=\; \max\{\, |x_k| \;:\; k < n \,\},$$

Assume AC, DC and countable choice for the Gaussian probability-law constructions below. The displayed finite real network recurrences and empirical loss are deterministic definitions for fixed parameters. Fix positive integers $d,n,H,m$, training inputs $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\|x_i\|_2=1$, labels $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$, an analytic nonpolynomial activation $\sigma$ satisfying $|\sigma(0)|<\infty$ and finite Lipschitz constants for $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$, and the positive finite normalization $c_\sigma=(\mathbb E_{Z\sim N(0,1)}[\sigma(Z)^2])^{-1}$. A fully connected network of width $m$ and depth $H$ is the finite feedforward recurrence

$$x^{(0)}=x,\qquad x^{(h)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(1\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm fc}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

where $W^{(1)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}$, $W^{(h)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for $h\ge2$, $a\in\mathbb R^m$, and $\sigma$ acts coordinatewise. The residual network uses the same first layer and then

$$x^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(1)}x),\qquad x^{(h)}=x^{(h-1)}+\frac{c_{\rm res}}{H\sqrt m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(2\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm res}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

with $0<c_{\rm res}<1$. In either architecture, random initialization means all entries of all matrices $W^{(h)}$ and of $a$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables; all these entries are trained by full-batch gradient descent. The empirical quadratic loss is $L(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(f(x_i,\theta)-y_i)^2$.

For the fully connected architecture and the same fixed data, define the population matrices by

$$K_{ij}^{(0)}=\langle x_i,x_j\rangle.$$

For $1\le h<H$, let $(U_{ij}^{(h)},V_{ij}^{(h)})$ be a centered bivariate normal vector with covariance

$$A_{ij}^{(h)}=\begin{pmatrix}K_{ii}^{(h-1)}&K_{ij}^{(h-1)}\\K_{ji}^{(h-1)}&K_{jj}^{(h-1)}\end{pmatrix},$$

and put $K_{ij}^{(h)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(U_{ij}^{(h)})\sigma(V_{ij}^{(h)})]$. For $h=H$, use the same bivariate-normal definition with $A_{ij}^{(H)}$ formed from $K^{(H-1)}$, and set

$$K_{ij}^{(H)}=c_\sigma K_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(U_{ij}^{(H)})\sigma'(V_{ij}^{(H)})].$$

When $H=1$, this last formula uses $K^{(0)}$ directly and there are no intermediate activation-covariance matrices. For the fully connected theorem, this terminal matrix is denoted $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$.

For the residual architecture with $H\ge2$, use a separate sequence $S^{(h)}$ and mean vector $b^{(h)}$. Set $S^{(0)}=K^{(0)}$. For $G^{(0)}\sim N_n(0,S^{(0)})$, put

$$S_{ij}^{(1)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})\sigma(G_j^{(0)})],\qquad b_i^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma}\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})].$$

Write $\alpha=c_{\rm res}/H$. For $2\le h<H$, take a fresh centered Gaussian vector $G^{(h-1)}$ with covariance $S^{(h-1)}$, put $\mu_i^{(h-1)}=\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})]$, and define

$$S_{ij}^{(h)}=S_{ij}^{(h-1)}+\alpha\bigl(b_i^{(h-1)}\mu_j^{(h-1)}+b_j^{(h-1)}\mu_i^{(h-1)}\bigr)+\alpha^2\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})\sigma(G_j^{(h-1)})],\qquad b_i^{(h)}=b_i^{(h-1)}+\alpha\mu_i^{(h-1)}.$$

For $G\sim N_n(0,S^{(H-1)})$, define the residual terminal matrix by

$$K_{{\rm res},ij}^{(H)}=\frac{c_{\rm res}^2}{H^2}S_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(G_i)\sigma'(G_j)].$$

The fully connected and residual convergence statements use $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$ and $K_{\rm res}^{(H)}$, respectively. At $H=1$, the two architectures coincide; define $K_{\rm res}^{(1)}=K_{\rm fc}^{(1)}$. The residual recursion above is the scalar specialization of the source's general mean/second-moment recursion, equation (16); in particular it includes the mean cross terms. Its terminal Gaussian covariance is $S^{(H-1)}$, as determined by the finite-width last-layer Gram formula (14).

The residual recurrence has one identity contribution from $x^{(h-1)}$ and one nonlinear contribution at every layer $2\le h\le H$; the arrows below depict that convention for one generic layer and do not enter any proof.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth,node distance=1.3cm]
  \node (in) {$x^{(h-1)}$};
  \node[draw,rectangle,right=1.7cm of in] (act) {$\frac{c_{\rm res}}{H\sqrt m}\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})$};
  \node[draw,circle,right=2.0cm of act] (sum) {$+$};
  \node[right=1.2cm of sum] (out) {$x^{(h)}$};
  \draw[->] (in) -- (act);
  \draw[->] (act) -- (sum);
  \draw[->] (in) to[bend right=28] (sum);
  \draw[->] (sum) -- (out);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

Assume AC, DC and countable choice. Under the hypotheses and notation defining the Du population Gram recursion, every fully connected matrix $K^{(h)}$, every residual feature second-moment matrix $S^{(h)}$, and both terminal matrices are finite, symmetric, and positive semidefinite. The fully connected matrices satisfy $K_{ii}^{(h)}=1$ for $0\le h<H$. For the residual sequence, $S^{(h)}-b^{(h)}(b^{(h)})^T$ is positive semidefinite for $1\le h<H$; its diagonal is not asserted to equal one.

Use either of the two architectures, its own terminal population kernel $K$, and independent Gaussian initialization. Assume AC, DC and countable choice and the activation and bounded-label hypotheses of the convergence theorems. Fix $0<\delta<1$. Write $\lambda=\lambda_{\min}(K)>0$, $q=1+\log(16/\delta)$ and $M=\sqrt{1+\log(16mnH/\delta)}$. There are constants $A\ge2$ and $C\ge1$, depending only on the fixed activation bounds, its normalizer, the label bound, and, in the residual case, $c_{\rm res}$, with the following property. For the fully connected case put $T=A^H$; if

$$m\ge C\max\{T n^4/\lambda^4,T n/\delta,T n^2\log(16Hn/\delta)/\lambda^2\},$$

then with probability at least $1-\delta$, simultaneously:

$$\max_{i,h}\|x_i^{(h)}(0)\|\le T,\quad \max_{h\ge2}\|W^{(h)}(0)\|_{\rm op}\le C\sqrt m,\quad \|a(0)\|_2\le C\sqrt m,\quad \|a(0)\|_4\le C m^{1/4},$$

$$\max_{i,h}\|b_{i,h}(0)\|_\infty\le T M,\quad \lambda_{\min}(J_H(0)J_H(0)^T)\ge3\lambda/4,\quad \|u(0)-y\|^2\le Tnq.$$

Here $J_H$ is the Jacobian block of the last hidden-layer matrix, and $b_{i,h}$ is the derivative of the scalar output with respect to the hidden feature vector $x_i^{(h)}$, so $b_{i,H}=a$. In the residual case $H\ge2$, the same conclusions hold with $T$ replaced everywhere in the conclusions by $C$, provided

$$m\ge C\max\{n^4H^6/\lambda^4,n^2/(\lambda^2H^2),n/\delta,n^2\log(16Hn/\delta)/\lambda^2\}.$$

For residual depth one use the fully connected case. Constants may be enlarged, and $A$ may be increased, simultaneously in these conclusions.

Fix finite real parameters obeying either Du architecture recurrence, with all parameters equipped with the Euclidean norm (Frobenius norm on each matrix block). At a fixed initialization assume all hidden feature norms are at most $B_x$, all matrices $W^{(h)}(0)$ with $h\ge2$ have operator norm at most $B_w\sqrt m$, $\|a(0)\|_2\le B_a\sqrt m$, $\|a(0)\|_4\le B_4m^{1/4}$, and all backward feature derivatives $b_{i,h}(0)=\nabla_{x_i^{(h)}}f_i$ have coordinate maxima at most $B_bM$, where $M\ge1$. For fully connected networks allow $B_x,B_b\le A_0^H$ for a fixed $A_0\ge2$, while $B_w,B_a,B_4$ are fixed independent of $H$. There are $A\ge2,C\ge1$ depending only on $A_0$, these fixed bounds and the activation, with the following bounds; write $T=A^H$. In the residual case the constants depend also on fixed $c_{\rm res}$, and every $T$ below is replaced by a fixed $C$ independent of $H$. Uniformly on any parameter ball $\|\theta-\theta_0\|\le D$ with $D/\sqrt m\le c/T$ (fully connected) or $D/\sqrt m\le c$ (residual),

$$\max_{i,h}\|x_i^{(h)}(\theta)-x_i^{(h)}(\theta_0)\|\le TD/\sqrt m,\qquad \|J(\theta)\|_{\rm op}\le T\sqrt n,$$

$$\max_i\|\nabla^2 f_i(\theta)\|_{\rm op}\le \frac{TM(1+D)}{\sqrt m},\qquad \|J_H(\theta)J_H(\theta)^T-J_H(\theta_0)J_H(\theta_0)^T\|_{\rm op}\le\frac{TnD}{\sqrt m}.$$

In the residual last inequality the upper bound is $CnD/(H^2\sqrt m)$ for $H\ge2$. The residual first-layer and output-vector derivatives are bounded without a factor $1/H$. Consequently, if $r_0=u(\theta_0)-y$ and $L=\frac12\|u-y\|^2$, the loss Hessian on the ball satisfies

$$\|\nabla^2L\|_{\rm op}\le Tn+\frac{T\sqrt n\,(\|r_0\|+T\sqrt nD)M(1+D)}{\sqrt m}.$$

The constants in this last bound can again be fixed independent of $H$ for residual networks. For any segment from $\theta$ to $\theta+h$ contained in the ball, its output Taylor remainder satisfies

$$\|u(\theta+h)-u(\theta)-J(\theta)h\|\le \frac{T\sqrt n M(1+D)}{2\sqrt m}\|h\|^2,$$

with $T$ replaced by fixed $C$ in the residual case.

Let $u:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$, $L=\frac12\|u-y\|^2$, and $r_0=u(\theta_0)-y$. On the closed ball $B(\theta_0,R)$ suppose a block $J_*$ of the output Jacobian satisfies $J_*J_*^T\succeq(\lambda/2)I_n$ and $\|\nabla^2L\|\le S$, with $\lambda,S>0$. If $R>2\sqrt2\|r_0\|/\sqrt\lambda$ and $0<\eta\le1/S$, every fixed-step gradient-descent iterate stays in the ball,

$$L(\theta_k)\le(1-\eta\lambda/2)^kL(\theta_0),\qquad\sum_{k\ge0}\|\theta_{k+1}-\theta_k\|\le2\sqrt2\|r_0\|/\sqrt\lambda.$$

The assertion is trivial for $r_0=0$; otherwise the hypotheses imply $0<\eta\lambda/2\le1$.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$
